definition: Repeatedly checking a device or software status to decide whether work is ready. The time between checks depends on the work the checking loop performs.
A function entered through the processor and SDK interrupt mechanism to handle an interrupt source. It should preserve required information and do bounded work before returning.
Temporarily preventing a class of interrupt requests from being accepted. Masking on one processor core does not by itself stop another core or every hardware actor.
An interrupt request recorded as waiting for service. A pending indication need not count every event that occurred while it was already pending.
A processor-specific ranking that helps determine which interrupt can be handled before or during another. Priority and masking affect response timing.
The delay between a relevant event or request and the chosen handler response point. State the measured endpoints and workload when using a latency number.
Hardware state that retains an indication after an event occurs, until the documented clearing action. One retained indication may merge several events.
A finite buffer that supplies retained items in their arrival order. If incoming data outpaces removal, the available storage can be exhausted.
Storage holding received bytes until software consumes them. Its capacity allows a limited delay but does not solve a sustained arrival rate above the consumption rate.

A receive error in which incoming data cannot all be retained because the receiving storage or service capacity is insufficient. Consult the device and driver for what is lost and how the condition is reported.

An application timing method that checks whether an interval has elapsed and then continues other work rather than waiting in a delay loop. It still depends on the time source and how often checks run.
A number that counts increments of a time source. Its unit and width must be known before interpreting it as elapsed time.
A finite unsigned counter whose next increment after its largest value produces zero. Two readings alone cannot identify how many complete counter cycles elapsed between them.
Integer arithmetic whose results are reduced into the unsigned type's representable range under the C conversion and arithmetic rules. Integer promotions and the actual expression types still matter.
A short operation protected from specified competing accesses. The protection must cover the actual actors that can change its shared data.
An overflow policy that stops a counter at a chosen limit rather than letting it wrap. An additional indicator may be needed to report that exact event counts were lost.
A hardware mechanism that transfers data without the processor executing an instruction for every data item. Interrupt masking on a CPU core does not inherently stop such a hardware transfer.
A processor event not blocked by the ordinary mask used for configurable interrupts. Its behaviour and available sources depend on the processor.
A peripheral that sends and receives serially framed data using local bit timing rather than a shared clock signal. Baud rate and frame settings do not define electrical voltage compatibility.
The number of transmitted symbols per second. For the binary UART signalling used in these lessons, one symbol carries one line bit, so the numerical baud and line-bit rates match.
A UART setting with eight data bits, no parity and one stop bit. Including the start bit, a byte occupies ten bit periods under the convention used here.
An optional UART checking bit derived from the data bits according to a selected convention. Both ends must agree whether it is used and how.
The UART framing bit that begins a serial character after the idle state. Its timing helps the receiver locate the character's data bits.
A configured UART framing interval after the data and optional parity bits. The frame format must match what the receiver expects.
Communication with a data path in each direction that can operate at the same time. It does not mean the application must always send useful data both ways.
Rules for finding the boundaries of application messages in received data, such as a terminator or a length field. UART character framing alone does not define these message boundaries.

A serial electrical interface with signal requirements different from typical microcontroller logic-level UART pins. Use a compatible interface or level-conversion hardware specified for the equipment.

Inter-Integrated Circuit: a serial bus using data and clock signals, addressing and acknowledgements. The ordinary bidirectional modes used here release lines high through pull-ups and drive them low.
The SDA signal carrying I2C address, data and acknowledgement information. Its permitted changes depend on the clock and bus conditions.
The SCL signal that coordinates I2C bit transfers. Clock stretching and electrical characteristics affect the observed timing in modes that permit them.
An I2C participant that initiates transfers and addresses targets. The lesson assumes one controller; the full specification also defines multi-controller operation.
An addressed participant in an I2C transfer. Its datasheet defines which command and data sequences it understands.
The device-selecting address bits before adding the transfer direction bit to the wire address byte. An API may expect this address rather than an already-shifted wire byte.
An I2C receiver response indicating acknowledgement of the preceding byte. It does not prove that the application-level contents are fresh or correct.
The I2C response in which a byte is not acknowledged. Its meaning depends on the phase: a controller-receiver normally sends it after the final requested data byte.
An I2C START condition issued without an intervening STOP, allowing a new address phase within a combined exchange. The target's protocol determines when this sequence is required.
An I2C participant extending a low clock interval in a mode that permits it. Driver support and timeouts must be checked for the actual devices.
A software or hardware decision to stop waiting when a chosen time bound is exceeded. It reports lack of timely progress; it does not by itself repair the cause.

A synchronous serial interface in which a controller supplies a clock and the connected device's protocol defines command framing. Common arrangements use separate data signals for each direction and a selection signal.
A signal used to select a peripheral or bound one of its exchanges according to that device's timing requirements. Active level and required timing are device-specific.
The controller-provided signal that sets SPI bit-transfer timing. Its idle level and sampling edge depend on the configured mode.
The SPI setting describing the idle clock level. It combines with clock phase to determine the sampling-edge convention.
The SPI setting selecting the sampling position relative to the leading and trailing clock edges. Read the device's mode and timing diagram rather than assuming an edge.
The SPI data direction from controller to peripheral. It is also commonly labelled MOSI using older controller/peripheral naming.
The SPI data direction from peripheral to controller. It is also commonly labelled MISO using older controller/peripheral naming.
A transmitted placeholder used to generate clocks while receiving a useful response in a device-specific exchange. Its permitted value and purpose come from the peripheral protocol.
Timing requirements specifying how long a relevant signal must be stable before and after a sampling or selection event. The relevant device's timing diagram defines the exact quantities.
The order in which the bits of a serial word are transferred, such as most-significant bit first. Both ends must use the device's required order.
The bit position with the greatest numeric weight in a binary value. In an MSB-first serial transfer this position is transmitted before the less-significant positions.
The bit position with the smallest numeric weight in a binary value. It is a position in the value, not a complete serial bit-order convention.
